records.name_note: All admissible sources consulted (NC State Extension, RHS, UF/IFAS) use "Persea americana" with no accepted-name conflict. NC State's structured plant record independently lists Genus: Persea, Species: americana, matching the binomial as given.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source addresses toxicity to dogs or cats specifically -- the animals this catalog's toxic_to_pets field tracks. RHS documents leaves as toxic to rabbits and fruit as harmful to pets including caged birds if eaten repeatedly (explicitly scoped to those animals, not "dogs, cats, rabbits" the way RHS phrases genuinely broad pet-toxicity claims elsewhere), and NC State separately flags a problem for horses. Left null rather than generalized to a flat true, consistent with how this catalog has treated horse-only or target-animal-scoped findings elsewhere (e.g. Elderberry in b28, Red Maple in b25).
records.cool_rest_note: Reduce watering in winter; keep the plant indoors at 13-18°C (55-65°F) and generally frost-free during the cold season.
unknowns: direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's "6 or more hours" text is the generic definition of its "Full sun" light category, reused across all NC State full-sun plant pages, not a measurement specific to avocado, so it was not used as a numeric value.
light_fc_min / light_fc_good: no admissible source (NC State, RHS, UF/IFAS) gives light levels in footcandles for this species.

soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: NC State checks all three of its pH category tags (Acid <6.0, Alkaline >8.0, Neutral 6.0-8.0) for this species, indicating broad tolerance, but these are open-ended category buckets, not specific numeric bounds, so no defensible min/max could be extracted.

water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a container/houseplant watering interval or check-depth. UF/IFAS (mg213) gives an in-ground landscape establishment watering frequency for young trees (twice weekly during dry periods) but that describes new-tree establishment in the ground, a different context from a potted plant's growing/dormant dry-down cycle, so it was not mapped to these fields.
humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: RHS states avocado 'likes humid air' but gives no percentage figure.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: RHS gives a propagation/active-growth temperature (20-25C / 68-77F) and a separate winter indoor minimum (13-18C / 55-65F), but frames these as growing-season vs. winter-season temperatures, not as a day/night (diurnal) split, so mapping them into day_f/night_f fields would misrepresent the source. The winter figure is instead reported qualitatively in cool_rest_note.

chill_damage_f: UF/IFAS (mg213) gives cold-damage thresholds for mature trees that vary sharply by horticultural race — West Indian 25-30F, Guatemalan 24-28F, Mexican race 18-26F — with no single species-wide damage-onset figure; picking one race's number would misrepresent the others, so this was left null rather than choosing a side.

fertilize_active_months / fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_strength: RHS says to feed 'during spring and summer' (a season, not named calendar months) at a dose/frequency deferred to the product packet, then 'every six to eight weeks' the rest of the year; UF/IFAS (mg213) gives a separate, non-matching in-ground landscape schedule (young trees every 1-2 months, mature trees 3-4 applications/year). These are inconsistent, context-differing schedules (houseplant vs. landscape tree) with no single clean figure supportable as one species-level value.

toxic_to_pets specifically for dogs and cats: no admissible source (NC State, RHS, UF/IFAS) addresses avocado toxicity to dogs or cats by name. Documented pet-toxicity from RHS is specific to rabbits (leaves) and caged birds (fruit, if eaten repeatedly), and NC State separately flags horses via a 'problem for horses' tag. Widely repeated claims that avocado is toxic to dogs/cats are not corroborated by any of the eight admissible publishers searched for this record.

Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page for Persea americana (plantfinder.mobot.org, taxonid=281661) could not be fetched due to a repeated TLS certificate verification error, so despite appearing in search results it was not used as a citation source for this record.

toxic_to_pets — corrected at landing: the batch's own audit passed this field through unrefuted, but its value rested entirely on RHS's rabbit- and bird-scoped citations plus NC State's horse tag -- no cat/dog evidence at all, despite the record's own toxicity_detail text explicitly saying so. This catalog has repeatedly ruled that a target-animal-scoped finding (no cats/dogs named) should null the field rather than generalize to true (Elderberry in b28, Red Maple in b25); this record was inconsistent with that precedent and is corrected to match it.

records.name_note: All admissible sources (NC State, Clemson, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS, Penn State, UF/IFAS, UGA) use the binomial Pyrus calleryana consistently for this species. RHS's own structured taxonomy field returns "Name Status: Correct" for Pyrus calleryana, and no admissible source proposes or defends a different accepted binomial. No conflict found, so scientific_name_accepted is retained as Pyrus calleryana.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: no admissible source affirmatively establishes pet toxicity for this species. RHS's page carries a 'Potentially harmful' section with an explicit 'Pets:' line reading 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten,' but this is RHS's standard fruit-ornamental caution -- it names no toxic principle, plant part, or symptom, and the same wording appears on many RHS ornamental-fruit-tree pages regardless of actual toxicity. No other admissible source (NC State, Clemson, Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UGA) addresses toxicity to pets at all, and none of the NC State page's standard Poison/Toxicity fields are populated for this species. Given the genuine ambiguity of the one source that does speak to it, left null rather than treated as an affirmative toxicity claim.

day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max: no admissible source gives ambient day/night temperature targets for this species; it is an outdoor hardy landscape tree, not a temperature-managed container plant, and only USDA winter-hardiness zone data is available (NC State 5a-9b; UF/IFAS 5A-9A; Missouri Botanical Garden Zone 5 to 9).

chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives a damage-onset cold temperature. The USDA hardiness-zone figures above are winter-survival floors, not the damage-onset figure this field calls for, so per instructions they were not mapped here.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source addresses a dormancy or chilling-requirement period for this species.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity for this outdoor tree.
light_fc_min, light_fc_good: no admissible source gives foot-candle light values.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and RHS's 'Position: Full sun' both define only a lower threshold for the full-sun category, not an upper bound, for this species.

soil_ph_min, soil_ph_max: NC State lists all three of its pH tolerance categories for this species -- 'Acid (<6.0)', 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)', and 'Alkaline (>8.0)' -- meaning the tree is described as tolerant across the full pH range with no floor or ceiling given by any admissible source, so neither numeric bound could be set.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a container-style watering schedule for this established, in-ground landscape tree. Missouri Botanical Garden's cultivar page gives only the qualitative field 'Water: Dry to medium,' and Clemson notes it 'tolerates most soil types and conditions, including occasional wet soils or drought' -- neither maps cleanly onto the container-oriented water_regime categories (keep_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between/keep_barely_moist).

fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: no admissible source gives a fertilizing schedule, interval, or dilution strength. Clemson's only fertility note is qualitative ('It requires low-to-medium fertility'), describing soil fertility tolerance rather than a feeding schedule.

Invasive/weedy status (no dedicated schema field, but explicitly called out as material to whether a home gardener should plant this species): NC State states plainly 'This plant is an invasive species in North Carolina' and lists 'Invasive Species... Weedy' among its Problems tags. Clemson states 'Pyrus calleryana and cultivars are on the Invasive Plant Pest Species of South Carolina list' and reports that as of October 1, 2024 all P. calleryana cultivars, including Bradford, were added to South Carolina's do-not-sell list. Penn State Extension opens its profile with 'Callery pear (Pyrus calleryana) is an invasive landscape tree' and separately confirms it has been 'on the Pennsylvania noxious weed list since 2024.' UF/IFAS assigns it 'Invasive and not recommended except for "specified and limited" use approved by the UF/IFAS Invasive Plant Working Group.' Missouri Botanical Garden's Bradford cultivar page carries a 'Midwest Noxious Weed: Do Not Plant' banner, stating it 'should not be moved or grown under conditions that would involve danger of dissemination. Not recommended for use in home gardens in the Midwest,' and separately notes 'concerns about invasiveness (non-sterile forms are escaping cultivation and naturalizing in some areas).' UGA CAES Field Report describes 'these wild-growing, invasive pear trees' as 'very common throughout the South.' No admissible source disputes the species' invasive status.

Weak branch structure / storm-damage susceptibility (no dedicated schema field, but explicitly called out as material to whether a home gardener should plant this species): every admissible source addressing structure flags the same weakness. NC State: 'The branches grow at upright angles with weak crotches that break with age, wind and ice.' Clemson: 'it does, however, suffer from severe branch splitting, especially in older trees (15+ years). The narrow branching angles cause trees to split in half, especially when subjected to ice and storm conditions,' and gives the tree only a 'short to moderate life span (15 to 25 years).' Missouri Botanical Garden: '"Bradford" is particularly susceptible to limb breakage or splitting from strong winds, snow or ice... it is now frequently not recommended by nurseries because of breakage potential... it should be considered to be a short-lived tree that may need to be replaced in 15-20 years.' UF/IFAS: 'The major problem with the `Bradford' callery pear has been too many upright branches growing too closely together on the trunk,' and by 'approach[ing] 20 years old, they begin to fall apart in ice and snow storms due to inferior, tight branch structure.' UGA CAES Field Report: 'these flowering pear trees tend to have a very weak, vertical branching structure that is notorious for splitting and breaking,' with most trees self-destructing under wind or storm loading by 10-20 years of age. No admissible source contradicts this.

unknowns — removed on audit: The invasive/weedy-status note embeds two specific dated regulatory claims that do not trace to any citation and are contradicted by the live cited pages. (1) It says Penn State Extension 'confirms it has been on the Pennsylvania noxious weed list since 2024' — I fetched https://extension.psu.edu/callery-pear directly (page last updated Feb 18, 2026) and it contains no mention of a noxious weed list, PA regulatory status, or the year 2024 anywhere; the only PSU quote actually present in the citations array is the generic 'is an invasive landscape tree' line. (2) It says Clemson 'reports that as of October 1, 2024 all P. calleryana cultivars, including Bradford, were added to South Carolina's do-not-sell list' — I fetched https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/bradford-pear/ directly and it contains no 'do-not-sell,' 'October,' or '2024' text anywhere; the only Clemson quote in the citations array is the generic 'Invasive Plant Pest Species of South Carolina list' line. Neither dated claim has a supporting citation entry at all. These are fabricated/unsourced insertions layered onto an otherwise well-supported note — the underlying general 'this species is widely flagged as invasive' claim remains soundly supported by the other six accurate citations (NC State, Clemson's general listing, Penn State's general 'invasive landscape tree' line, UF/IFAS, Missouri Botanical Garden, UGA), so only these two specific sub-claims are refuted, not the note as a whole.

records.name_note: NC State Extension lists this species' prior names as "Ulmus americana var. americana, Ulmus americana var. floridana, Ulmus floridana" -- these were folded into Ulmus americana rather than pointing to a different currently-accepted taxon. RHS's own Ulmus americana taxon page independently shows Name Status: Correct. No admissible source proposes a different currently-accepted binomial for this species, so there is no conflict to resolve.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max/humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max/light_fc_min/light_fc_good/cool_rest_note: left null. These read as indoor-microclimate and container-culture fields; no admissible source discusses ambient day/night temperature, humidity, foot-candle light levels, or a dormancy/cool-rest period for this outdoor, fully cold-hardy landscape tree (USDA Zones 2A-9B per UF/IFAS, 3a-9b per NC State).

direct_sun_hours_max: left null. NC State's parenthetical '(6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' / '(Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' is the site's fixed, generic legend text defining its Full Sun/Partial Shade categories -- this catalog has already confirmed elsewhere, via direct fetch of unrelated species pages, that this exact wording is reused verbatim site-wide rather than a measured or species-curated sun-hours figure -- so the number 6 was not extracted from it as a distinct data point for Ulmus americana specifically.

chill_damage_f: left null. No admissible source states a specific sublethal damage-onset temperature. UF/IFAS gives 'USDA hardiness zones: 2A through 9B' and NC State gives '3a, 3b, 4a, 4b, 5a, 5b, 6a, 6b, 7a, 7b, 8a, 8b, 9a, 9b' -- both are survival/hardiness-zone floors, not a stated point where sublethal chill damage begins, so per instructions they were not mapped onto this field.

soil_drainage: left null. Admissible sources describe very broad, near-opposite drainage tolerance rather than one regime: NC State's own Soil Drainage tags list 'Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry, Occasionally Wet, Very Dry' simultaneously; Missouri Botanical Garden's Culture note says to grow in 'well-drained soils' while separately stating the tree 'Adapts to both wet and dry sites'; and UF/IFAS's Soil tolerances run 'wet to well-drained.' Given tolerance spanning nearly the whole spectrum, no single fast/moderate/moisture_retentive value was chosen.

water_regime and water_dry_down_target: left null. This field is treated as harm-capable, and no admissible source recommends either keeping soil consistently moist or letting it dry down between waterings -- the consistent theme across NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, and UF/IFAS is that the species tolerates wet and dry sites about equally once established, which does not cleanly match any single regime option, so no side was picked.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: left null. No admissible source frames watering as a checkable numeric schedule (a soil-probe depth or a day interval) for this in-ground, established landscape tree.

fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: left null. No admissible source gives any fertilizer schedule, calendar month, or dilution/strength guidance specific to Ulmus americana.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail: left null. No admissible source addresses toxicity to pets or humans for this species. Unlike many other entries in NC State's Plant Toolbox, the Ulmus americana page carries no 'Poison'-prefixed structured fields or toxicity tags at all, and none of Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS, UF/IFAS (ENH-806/ST649), or Clemson's Elm factsheet (HGIC 1011) mention a toxic principle, plant part, or symptom for this species.

Clemson Cooperative Extension's 'Elm' factsheet (HGIC 1011) is a genus-wide overview page: its light and soil-tolerance guidance ('Elms prefer full sun to part shade... they adapt to most soil conditions') is written about 'elms'/'most elms' collectively, not Ulmus americana specifically, so it was not used as a citation for outdoor_sun_exposure or soil fields here -- those fields are instead supported by NC State's and UF/IFAS's species-specific pages, which name Ulmus americana directly and reach the same full-sun/partial-shade conclusion independently.

RHS's Ulmus americana profile page is a minimal stub (only Family, a genus-level description, Name Status, and common names are populated) -- it provided the Name Status Correct data point used for scientific_name_accepted but no cultivation data (no height, sun, soil, or hardiness fields), so it neither corroborates nor conflicts with any other field here.

water_regime: left null because none of the schema's four enum values (keep_moist, dry_surface_between, dry_thoroughly_between, keep_barely_moist) cleanly describes an established, drought-tolerant landscape tree's watering profile. Clemson states 'Once established, live oak is drought-resistant' and UF/IFAS rates 'Drought tolerance: high'; NC State's structured Soil Drainage field ('Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry') describes soil moisture tolerance, not a watering cadence. Forcing this into a container/garden-style watering schedule would misrepresent the sources.

chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives a specific damage-onset temperature. Only USDA hardiness-zone survival ranges are given (NC State: 8a-10b; UF/IFAS: 7B-10B; RHS: H6, 'hardy in all of UK and northern Europe (-20 to -15)'), which describe survivability, not an actionable cold-damage threshold. Clemson notes the species can suffer 'ice storm damage' in NC's mountains but gives no temperature figure.

cool_rest_note: no admissible source describes a distinct cool/dormancy-rest care regimen; live oak is repeatedly described as evergreen/semi-evergreen (retains leaves until new ones emerge in spring) rather than having a winter dormancy period requiring special care.

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: NC State is the only admissible source addressing toxicity for this species, and its poisoning profile (Poison Severity: Low; toxic principle gallotannins, quercitrin, and quercitin; parts Leaves and Seeds; symptoms stomach pain, constipation, bloody diarrhea, excessive thirst) is filed entirely under a 'Poisonous to Humans' heading, per the rule against blending human-only toxicity data into the pets field. NC State separately tags the page '#problem for horses' but supplies no severity, symptom, or toxic-principle data tied to that tag, and horses are a different animal target from dogs/cats in any case. Clemson, RHS, and UF/IFAS do not mention toxicity for this species at all. No admissible source names dogs or cats specifically, so both fields are left null.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: left null because no admissible source gives a specific numeric pH range for this species. soil_base garden_bed: supported by NC State ('It makes a magnificent shade tree for large areas with a broad spreading canopy'), UF/IFAS's Uses list ('street without sidewalk; shade; specimen; reclamation; parking lot island...'), and Clemson ('Live oak does well as a lawn specimen when provided plenty of space to grow') -- all describing an in-ground landscape/shade-tree growing context, the closest schema match; no admissible source discusses container culture for this species.

soil_drainage moderate: no admissible source uses the schema's literal categories (fast/moderate/moisture_retentive). 'moderate' is inferred from consistently 'well-drained' language paired with moisture tolerance across NC State ('Good Drainage,' 'Moist,' 'Occasionally Dry'), UF/IFAS ('well-drained' alongside 'occasionally wet'), RHS ('Moist but well-drained'), and Clemson ('well-drained, sandy soils with plenty of moisture' while also tolerating 'drier, more compacted soils') -- reading as neither fast/gritty drainage nor constantly moisture-retentive, consistent with how this same categorical inference was made for the sibling species Quercus alba (White Oak) already in this catalog.

Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder (plantfinder.mobot.org) was searched but has no dedicated page for Quercus virginiana; no citation was taken from that domain. Penn State Extension (extension.psu.edu), University of Maryland Extension (extension.umd.edu), and UGA CAES Field Report (fieldreport.caes.uga.edu) were also searched but did not surface species-specific cultivation pages for Quercus virginiana; no citations were taken from those domains.

Purely descriptive horticultural details with no corresponding schema field (mature height/spread figures ranging roughly 40-120 ft depending on source and setting, growth rate of about 2-2.5 ft/year, lifespan of 200-300 years, bark/leaf/acorn morphology, wildlife and pollinator value, pest and disease notes, root damage to nearby pavement) are well-documented across the four sources used but are omitted here because the catalog schema has no field for them, not because they are unsupported.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The two citations backing 'accepted' status don't actually establish acceptance independent of the already-used given-name evidence. Citation 5 (NC State 'Genus: Quercus Species: virginiana') is a verbatim re-use of the same structured field already cited for scientific_name_given ('Scientific Name: Quercus virginiana') -- it shows the source uses this binomial, not that it has been checked against synonymy/taxonomic-authority status, so it's circular support for a field that's conceptually distinct from 'given name'. That leaves citation 4 (RHS quote 'Name Status: Correct') as the sole citation actually asserting an acceptance determination, and 'Name Status: Correct' is not a field label that appears on RHS's standard public plant-profile display (which shows Genus/Species/Family/Hardiness-type fields, not an explicit accepted/synonym status flag) -- so its literal presence on that page is unverified. With one citation circular and the other's literal quote of doubtful provenance, the 'accepted' (as opposed to merely 'given') designation is not solidly established by admissible sources.

soil_base — removed on audit: All three citations describe a 60-80 ft canopy shade/street/highway-median tree ('magnificent shade tree for large areas', 'street without sidewalk; shade; specimen; reclamation; ... highway median', 'lawn specimen when provided plenty of space') -- none use language matching 'garden_bed', and unlike is_houseplant there is no clean, unproblematic citation among the three that directly maps to that specific category. 'Garden bed' ordinarily connotes a cultivated bed for shrubs/perennials/smaller ornamentals, not a forest-canopy shade tree used as a street or median planting. The unknowns note itself concedes this is only the 'closest schema match' -- i.e. the value itself, not just one supporting citation, is in doubt.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: 'Moderate' is not literally stated by any of the four sources, and the record blends two different kinds of data to get there. NC State's own structured field lists 'Good Drainage' as a distinct checkbox from the separate moisture-tolerance checkboxes 'Moist'/'Occasionally Dry' -- 'Good Drainage' alone maps more naturally to a fast/well-drained category than to 'moderate'. UF/IFAS's 'well-drained' plus 'occasionally wet' and RHS's/Clemson's 'well-drained' language are similarly drainage-rate-plus-moisture-tolerance blends, not a stated 'moderate' rate. Because every citation requires the same inferential blending rather than one clean citation carrying the value, this is a value-level uncertainty, and the categorical choice is an interpretive call rather than one directly backed by any source's literal wording.

name_note — removed on audit: The clause 'likely reflecting its limited winter hardiness for the St. Louis area' -- offered as the explanation for why Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder has no page for this species -- is not attributed to or supported by any citation in the record. It is the researcher's own unsourced conjecture about causation, inserted inline with otherwise-sourced factual statements in a way that could be mistaken for cited content.

records.name_note: No accepted-name conflict among admissible sources: NC State's structured Attributes block reads "Genus: Datura Species: stramonium Family: Solanaceae," and RHS's Name Status field for Datura stramonium reads "Correct." NC State separately lists four historical synonyms under "Previously known as: Datura inermis Datura stramonium f. godronii Datura tatula Stramonium vulgatum," none of which is proposed by any source as a current accepted alternative. A common-name ambiguity is worth flagging explicitly, since this record is a deliberate companion to Brugmansia (Angel's Trumpet) already in this catalog: NC State Extension's own site catalogs "Jimsonweed" as the primary common name not only for this species but also, on a separate page, for the related-but-distinct species Datura wrightii ("Jimsonweed - Datura wrightii"), and that Datura wrightii page in turn (a) lists "Angel's Trumpet" among its own other common names, (b) lists "Brugmansia" itself among the genera it "is often confused with," and (c) explicitly cross-references this species with the line "Other plants called Jimsonweed: Datura stramonium." This record covers only Datura stramonium, confirmed by NC State's own species-level Genus/Species attribute fields quoted above; no content from the Datura wrightii page or any Brugmansia source was used for any field in this record.
records.toxicity_detail: All parts of the plant are treated as toxic to people, pets, and livestock. NC State Extension's Description states plainly, "If ingested, it is a dangerous and toxic plant for humans, pets, and livestock," and its general problems note (filed separately from the page's human-specific poison-detail block) adds: "All parts of this plant are toxic if ingested. Keep out of reach of small children and pets. The sap can cause skin irritation, and protective clothing and gloves are recommended when handling this plant." NC State's own structured "Problems:" attribute list separately names "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," "Problem for Horses," and "Weedy" alongside "Poisonous to Humans" -- these are genuinely animal-specific tags in their own right, distinct from the page's separate "Poisonous to Humans:" heading and its Poison Severity/Symptoms/Toxic Principle/Poison Part fields, which are not used here (see unknowns). RHS's plant profile for this species carries its own "TOXIC to pets" tag alongside "TOXIC if eaten; skin irritant; avoid eye contact. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling," and its separate Thorn Apple weeds-advice page states "All parts of the plant are poisonous – wear gloves when handling and wash your hands" and separately warns that gardeners "may wish to get rid of thorn apple if there is any risk that children or pets may eat or handle some." For livestock specifically, UGA Cooperative Extension's toxic-pasture-weed guide names the toxic chemicals as "the tropane alkaloids atropine, hyoscyamine, and scopolamine," states "All parts of the plant are toxic, whether green or dry but the seeds are the most poisonous," and reports that cattle and pigs are the most affected livestock, with "Nearly any level of consumption is lethal to pigs while cattle may be able to withstand up to 14 oz per 1,000 lbs. of bodyweight." Penn State Extension similarly states of the species generally: "all parts of the plant are poisonous to animals and humans. It has been ingested in various forms as a hallucinogenic drug, but the alkaloids are extremely dangerous and should not be consumed." UF/IFAS's horse-focused toxic-plant guide lists jimsonweed only in a closing summary of secondary-risk plants, noting these species "are typically avoided by horses, or large quantities are required to cause toxicity" -- a palatability/practical-risk nuance for horses specifically, not a contradiction of the toxicity determination itself.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: null. NC State's Soil pH tags check all three of 'Acid (<6.0),' 'Neutral (6.0-8.0),' and 'Alkaline (>8.0),' and RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' -- both span the entire pH scale with no numeric preference expressed as this species' actual target.

NC State's only relevant line -- 'This fast-growing plant thrives in full sun and moist, well-drained soils of almost any type, but prefers humus-rich soil. They are drought-tolerant once established and sensitive to frost' -- mixes a moist-soil preference with an explicit drought-tolerance qualifier and reads as a soil-type/establishment note rather than a clean watering directive either way. No admissible source gives a numeric check-depth or day-interval watering schedule, so these fields were left null rather than guessed given the genuine internal tension in the one relevant sentence available.

No admissible source addresses feeding this plant at all; every source treats it exclusively as a toxic weed to identify, avoid, or remove, never as a plant with a feeding program -- consistent with how this catalog treated Poison Ivy and Pokeweed.

is_houseplant: set to false rather than left null because the schema field is a required boolean. No admissible source describes indoor or container culture for this species; NC State's own Landscape Location tag is 'Naturalized Area' (an outdoor-only category), and every other admissible source used here (RHS's weeds-advice page, UMD, UGA, Penn State) treats the plant exclusively as an outdoor weed to identify and control, never as something grown indoors.

soil_base garden_bed: an inferential enum mapping, not a literal quote match -- no source uses that phrase. Chosen because the plant is repeatedly described as growing in open ground ('thrives in full sun and moist, well-drained soils of almost any type,' NC State; 'Can be used for summer bedding in fertile, well-drained soil with full sun,' RHS) and none of this catalog's container/potting-mix soil_base categories (standard_potting, chunky_aroid, cactus_succulent, ericaceous, orchid_bark, african_violet, semi_hydro) fit an outdoor, self-seeding annual weed.

soil_drainage moderate: also an inferential mapping, from NC State's 'Good Drainage, Moist' tags and RHS's 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained' field. RHS's alternate standalone 'Well-drained' option was not treated as pointing toward 'fast' given the co-listed 'Moist but well-drained' phrasing is listed first and is echoed by NC State's own separate 'Moist' tag.

toxicity_detail deliberately excludes NC State's detailed 'Poisonous to Humans:' block (Poison Severity: High; the specific symptom list of dilated pupils/fever/hallucinations/delirium/coma; Poison Toxic Principle; Poison Part list). Direct fetch of the page's underlying markup confirms this entire block sits under its own 'Poisonous to Humans:' group heading, structurally separate from the page's other 'Problems:' attribute list (which does separately, and legitimately, name Cats/Dogs/Horses as distinct entries). Consistent with how this catalog handled the identical distinction for Pokeweed and Brugmansia, the human-headed severity/symptom/toxic-principle narrative was not carried into this animal-facing field; the toxic-principle chemical names used instead come from UGA's livestock-facing (cattle/pigs) pasture-weed guide, a source not gated to a human-only heading.

UF/IFAS's VM247 ('Common Toxic Plants for Florida Horse Owners') names jimsonweed only in a closing summary sentence about secondary-risk plants ('typically avoided by horses, or large quantities are required to cause toxicity') -- included in toxicity_detail as a horse-specific palatability nuance, not used to weaken or contradict toxic_to_pets, since no source disputes that ingestion itself is toxic.

name_note / common-name overlap: this record is confirmed to be Datura stramonium specifically (NC State's own Genus/Species attribute fields), not the separate species Datura wrightii, which NC State's site also files under the common name 'Jimsonweed' and which itself carries 'Angel's Trumpet' as one of its other common names and lists 'Brugmansia' among genera it is confused with. No content from either the Datura wrightii page or any Brugmansia source was used for this record.

Clemson HGIC (hgic.clemson.edu) was searched specifically; no dedicated Datura stramonium/jimsonweed page was found. The only close hit, 'October Week 3 Plants,' is a photo-gallery page whose caption mislabels this species as 'Angel's Trumpet (Datura stramonium)' with no accompanying care detail; given both the mislabeling and the complete absence of care content, it was not used as a citation. Clemson's 'Growing Annuals' factsheet lists only 'Thorn Apple (Datura species)' among fragrant annuals, again with no species-specific or care detail.

Missouri Botanical Garden (plantfinder.mobot.org / missouribotanicalgarden.org) was searched specifically; no dedicated Datura stramonium page exists on either domain -- only pages for the related species Datura metel and Datura inoxia, which were not used since they are different species from the one covered by this record.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The record sets soil_drainage="moderate" on two citations — NC State's structured tag "Soil Drainage: Good Drainage Moist" and RHS's structured field "Moisture: Moist but well–drained or Well–drained" (both re-verified live: NC State's Attributes block reads exactly "Soil Drainage: Good Drainage; Moist", RHS's reads exactly "Soil Moisture: Moist but well–drained or Well–drained"). Neither quote contains the word "moderate" or a clean synonym for a medium-drainage tier as distinct from fast or moisture-retentive drainage. This is not a novel judgment call: this exact citation pattern — NC State's "Good Drainage"+"Moist" tag pair combined with RHS's "Moist but well-drained or Well-drained" field — has been explicitly audited and rejected as unsupported for "moderate" repeatedly elsewhere in this same catalog (app/data/verified/b17-perennials3.json:50, b18-perennials4.json:54, b23-daylily-and-more-gaps.json:469 and :723, b14-annual-flowers2.json:1204, b12-fruit-and-flowers1.json:50, b11-veg-round4.json:51), with b23's own audit note stating the policy explicitly: "well-drained" + "moist"/"organically rich" language that never uses the schema's literal fast/moderate/moisture_retentive wording should be "left null rather than force a category," and that "forcing it to 'moderate' was rejected on audit for a different species on the same grounds." The Jimsonweed record repeats the identical previously-rejected mapping. Per this catalog's own established precedent the correct disposition is null, not "moderate."

records.name_note: NC State Extension and RHS agree the currently accepted name for this species is Curio radicans; Senecio radicans, the name given for this record, is listed by both as an earlier name. NC State also notes the genus name Curio derives from Latin curiosus ("curious", for the plant's odd form) and the epithet radicans means "taking root"; the same source notes this species is related to Curio rowleyanus, known as string-of-pearls.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension rates this species "low severity" poison. Its Poison Symptoms text explicitly names pets and livestock alongside humans, rather than staying silent about them: "Toxic if ingested by humans, pets, or livestock: loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting. If large amounts are ingested, it can cause irreversible liver disease." The toxic principle is pyrrolizidine alkaloids, found in the flowers, fruits, leaves, roots, sap/juice, seeds, and stems. Separately, the sap causes contact dermatitis ("Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes"), matching the plant's own "Contact Dermatitis" problem tag. This data sits under a "Poisonous to Humans" section header on NC State's page, but unlike the header-only pattern this catalog treats with suspicion elsewhere, the symptom sentence itself broadens the claim to pets and livestock by name. It does not, however, break the symptoms out by animal species the way some other NC State pages do, so no cat-only or dog-only symptom is asserted here -- one shared symptom set is reported instead.
records.water_dry_down_target: Water only once the top half of the soil has dried out, not merely the surface. NC State Extension: "Water the plant only when the top half of the soil feels dry ... It is drought tolerant and over-watering needs to be avoided."

normalizations: 2026-08-23: thirteenth batch of the "blind spots" pass. Avocado (a fruit + houseplant crossover, since people commonly sprout the pit) and Jimsonweed (a deliberate companion to Angel's Trumpet/Brugmansia, already in this catalog -- same tropane-alkaloid family, uncultivated-weed framing matching how this catalog already treated poison ivy and pokeweed in b30). Rounded out with Bradford Pear, American Elm, Southern Live Oak, String of Bananas (distinct from String of Pearls, already covered), a small true Air Plant (distinct from Spanish Moss, already covered), and American Persimmon (edible-ripe/astringent-unripe, with a separately documented horse phytobezoar risk this batch's species note specifically asked to keep distinct from ingestion poisoning).

One landing-time correction, not caught by this batch's own audit: Avocado's toxic_to_pets was set true, but its own citations only support rabbit- and caged-bird-specific harm (RHS, explicitly scoped -- notably NOT phrased "dogs, cats, rabbits" the way RHS writes genuinely broad pet-toxicity claims elsewhere, e.g. Azalea in b19) plus a horse tag (NC State) -- no cat/dog evidence anywhere, which the record's own toxicity_detail text already admitted in prose. This catalog has twice already ruled that a target-animal-scoped finding with no cat/dog data should null the field rather than generalize to true (Elderberry in b28, Red Maple in b25); corrected to match that precedent.

The audit caught something more serious than a citation-quality issue on Bradford Pear: two specific, dated regulatory claims ("Pennsylvania noxious weed list since 2024"; "South Carolina do-not-sell list effective October 1, 2024") that don't appear anywhere on the actual cited Penn State or Clemson pages -- fabricated specifics layered onto an otherwise accurate general invasive-species note. Caught by direct re-fetch, not just citation-matching, and removed while the soundly-supported general invasive-species finding (from six other accurate citations) was kept.

Jimsonweed's soil_drainage catch shows the audit now enforcing cross-batch consistency at real scale: the same "Good Drainage" + "Moist"/"well-drained" citation pattern mapped to 'moderate' here has already been explicitly audited and rejected across seven other records in this catalog (b11, b12, b14, b17, b18, and twice in b23) -- the audit cited each by file:line and applied the same established rule rather than treating this as a fresh judgment call.
